newsitem.title: FRANCE: Cr Lyonnais to report earnings, state aid to help.
newsitem.headline: Cr Lyonnais to report earnings, state aid to help.

text.p: Ailing Credit Lyonnais reports its half-year earnings on Thursday, helped by another hefty dose of public money aimed at saving the bank from plunging back into the red.

Banking analysts estimate state-controlled Credit Lyonnais, which the government has said it wants to privatise as soon as possible, could post up to a 500 million franc ($96.8 million) profit for the first six months following last week's announcement of a 3.9 billion franc state emergency aid package for the bank.
It reported a 36 million franc profit for the corresponding year-earlier period.

The results were delayed for a week to give Prime Minister Alain Juppe's conservative government time to win approval from the European Commission for the emergency help. Without it, the bank was expected to post a loss of at least two billion francs.

The aid was designed to remove the burden of costs imposed on Credit Lyonnais as part of last year's bailout. The government said it would be followed by a full-blown state rescue, the third in three years, to ready the bank for sale.

The burden was imposed to make Credit Lyonnais share the cost of an expansion binge which briefly made it the biggest bank outside Japan before bringing about its near collapse. But the terms proved too harsh in a depressed banking climate.
The bank eked out a 13 million franc profit for 1995 after racking up losses of 21 billion francs between 1992 and 1994.
The government said it would wait until the half-year figures to decide how much more public money it would pump into the bank but the sum is expected to be around 10 billion francs.

By conservative estimates, taking into account the two 1994 and 1995 rescues, the ultimate bill to taxpayers for keeping the bank afloat is expected to hit at least 100 billion francs with some analysts estimating it could run as high as 125 billion.

Analysts cautioned even if the half-year figures were good, there was still huge uncertainty about the bank's future. The European Commission is expected to impose tough conditions on the bank in exchange for approving the fresh state aid.
No clear suitors have yet emerged for the bank's hand.

The bank, which was ordered to divest many of its assets in exchange for European Commission approval of the second bailout, could be forced to spin off even more, including some of its cherished money spinners.

"Even if the figures are good tomorrow, it will not give any answers about what the supranational authority will decide. There is a complete lack of transparency about this," said one Paris analyst. "Its destiny is not in its hands." ($ = 5.166 French Francs)
